title: The 2026 Healthcare AI ROI Scorecard
gist: Bessemer and Bain's 2026 survey of 226 healthcare executives finds AI ROI arriving in ~12 months at ~3.5x, concentrated in administrative work like revenue cycle (4.0x, 67% autonomous agents) while clinical AI (2.9x, 4% autonomous) is held back by trust, liability, regulation and reimbursement. Buyers are abandoning internal builds and consolidating vendors, favoring healthcare-specific AI startups, with multi-trillion-dollar opportunities remaining in payer-provider admin friction, clinical care and drug development.

insights.claim: In Bessemer and Bain's 2026 survey of 226 healthcare executives, 71% say GenAI has already transformed clinical treatment decisions, versus 84% in 2025 who expected it to within three to five years.
insights.speaker: Bessemer Venture Partners
insights.so_what: Healthcare AI adoption is running ahead of multi-year forecasts, pulling forward vendor revenue timelines.
insights.quote: In 2025, 84% expected GenAI to transform clinical treatment decisions within three to five years. One year later, 71% say it already has.
insights.locator: Last year, 408 healthcare executives told

insights.claim: Healthcare AI buyers projected roughly 24 months to ROI but realized it in about 12 months, averaging a 3.5x return and exceeding expectations in about 40% of use cases, with 54% seeing material ROI inside the first year.
insights.speaker: Bessemer Venture Partners
insights.so_what: Faster-than-underwritten payback supports budget expansion and shortens sales cycles for proven vendors.
insights.quote: Buyers projected ~24 months, and realized it in ~12, averaging 3.5x, exceeding expectations in ~40% of use cases. 54% see material ROI inside the first year.
insights.locator: Healthcare AI ROI arrived twice as fast

insights.claim: Because nearly every healthcare AI budget of the past two years assumed a two-year payback that proved wrong by half, organizations still modeling two-year paybacks are underinvesting relative to their own results.
insights.speaker: Bessemer Venture Partners
insights.so_what: Expect upward revisions to healthcare AI budgets as buyers recalibrate payback assumptions.
insights.quote: Organizations still modeling two-year paybacks are underinvesting against their own results.
insights.locator: ROI is arriving twice as fast

insights.claim: Realized healthcare AI ROI by function: provider revenue cycle 4.0x, payer claims and pharma preclinical discovery 3.4x, payer provider network 3.3x, member engagement 3.2x, provider front office 3.1x, provider clinical 2.9x, pharma commercial 2.6x, clinical development 2.3x.
insights.speaker: Bessemer Venture Partners
insights.so_what: The ranking tells where to allocate capital first: revenue cycle and claims vendors have the strongest proven economics.
insights.locator: Provider revenue cycle: 4.0X.

insights.claim: Bessemer views the reported returns as a floor rather than a ceiling because they are realized on roughly two-year-old deployments, and planned headcount reductions that convert automation into permanent savings are largely not yet executed.
insights.speaker: Bessemer Venture Partners
insights.so_what: Additional cost savings are still in the pipeline, implying further ROI uplift and vendor expansion.
insights.quote: we see them as a floor rather than a ceiling
insights.locator: This is based on realized ROI

insights.claim: Every surveyed healthcare function clears or approaches the 3x return threshold enterprise buyers typically require before funding at scale, so the decision shifts from whether to fund AI to which function to fund first.
insights.speaker: Bessemer Venture Partners
insights.so_what: Funding prioritization, not approval, becomes the gating factor for vendor sales.
insights.quote: The decision is no longer whether to fund AI; rather, the ROI ranking tells executives which function to fund first.
insights.locator: Every function we surveyed clears

insights.claim: Administrative AI ROI is driven by speed to output, increased revenue and reduced FTE cost that land within a single budget year, whereas clinical AI value so far comes from optimized decision-making and improved quality, explaining most of the ROI gap.
insights.speaker: Bessemer Venture Partners
insights.so_what: Clinical AI vendors face harder value attribution, lengthening sales cycles versus admin tools.
insights.locator: But not all returns are the same.

insights.claim: Pharma is earliest on the ROI Scorecard because attributing value is hard when drug development timelines dwarf a one-year measurement window.
insights.speaker: Bessemer Venture Partners
insights.so_what: Pharma AI returns will be under-reported in short windows; investors should use longer horizons.
insights.quote: attributing value is genuinely hard when drug timelines dwarf a one-year measurement window
insights.locator: The ROI Scorecard is the successor

insights.claim: Use cases in the top-left of the ROI Scorecard, with proven returns but low adoption, are where the next wave of healthcare AI adoption is most likely to come from.
insights.speaker: Bessemer Venture Partners
insights.so_what: Look for vendors in high-ROI, low-adoption use cases for the next growth leg.
insights.quote: The top-left quadrant is worth paying attention to as it’s where the next wave of adoption is most likely to come from.
insights.locator: How to read the scorecard

insights.claim: Two-thirds of provider revenue cycle respondents run semi- or fully autonomous AI agents and 62% do so in payer member engagement, versus only 4% in provider clinical work.
insights.speaker: Bessemer Venture Partners
insights.so_what: Agentic AI revenue is concentrated in administrative workflows; clinical autonomy remains a distant market.
insights.quote: Where organizations have handed the work over entirely, they have handed over administrative work.
insights.locator: Autonomy is the tell.

insights.claim: Every adoption gain of consequence in 2026 was administrative: payer contracting management rose from 19% to 37%, provider credentialing and enrollment from 35% to 56%, provider contracting from 40% to 60%, and prior authorization from 32% to 46%.
insights.speaker: Bessemer Venture Partners
insights.so_what: Contracting, credentialing and prior-auth tooling are the fastest-growing healthcare AI categories.
insights.quote: Every adoption gain of consequence this year was administrative.
insights.locator: Why the money landed in admin

insights.claim: Clinical AI reaches proof of concept at the same rate as administrative AI but converts to full deployment at half that rate, held back by trust, liability and reimbursement rather than model capability.
insights.speaker: Bessemer Venture Partners
insights.so_what: Clinical AI bottlenecks are institutional, not technical; better models alone will not unlock the market.
insights.quote: held back not by model capability but by trust, liability, and reimbursement
insights.locator: In 2026, the answer split in two

insights.claim: Between 2025 and 2026 pilots rose across segments (provider 21% to 28%, pharma 20% to 31%, payer 19% to 24%) while production barely moved (provider 8% to 12%, pharma 5% to 6%, payer flat at 6%).
insights.speaker: Bessemer Venture Partners
insights.so_what: Few organizations have crossed into production, leaving a large conversion opportunity for vendors that can deploy at scale.
insights.locator: Use cases across the implementation curve

insights.claim: Over half of next year's incremental healthcare AI investment will go to deployment: 35% to scaling proven use cases and 20% to workflow integration, versus 13% for infrastructure and 11% for foundation model licensing.
insights.speaker: Bessemer Venture Partners
insights.so_what: Spend favors deployment and integration vendors over infrastructure and model licensing.
insights.quote: 35% to scaling proven use cases and 20% to integrating them into existing workflows, against 13% for infrastructure and 11% for foundation model licensing
insights.locator: Over half of next year's incremental

insights.claim: With 72% of healthcare organizations now having an AI governance committee, AI purchasing decisions are increasingly centralized, and regulatory and compliance uncertainty is expected to be the top driver of delayed or canceled deployments.
insights.speaker: Bessemer Venture Partners
insights.so_what: Centralized procurement favors compliant, platform-scale vendors and lengthens point-solution sales.
insights.locator: Regulatory and compliance uncertainty will be

insights.claim: Providers and pharma are furthest along in scaling vetted AI solutions, while payers are still in ideation; the largest moves into production were front-office provider (14%), RCM provider (10%) and member services payer (10%).
insights.speaker: Bessemer Venture Partners
insights.so_what: Payer AI is an earlier-stage market with more greenfield opportunity.
insights.locator: 2025 was the year of the PoC

themes.theme: Vendor consolidation and death of internal build

insights.claim: 61% of healthcare organizations report that half or fewer of their internally built AI tools are still maintained and in use, and 32% report less than a quarter survived.
insights.speaker: Bessemer Venture Partners
insights.so_what: Internal builds are failing at production; external vendors capture the replacement demand.
insights.locator: The era of the internal build

insights.claim: Internal AI builds fail not at building but at operating at production reliability, monitoring, keeping current with changing models and standing behind outputs in audits, so the internal share of development fell by 16 points.
insights.speaker: Bessemer Venture Partners
insights.so_what: Vendors that own maintenance, monitoring and auditability have a durable moat over in-house teams.
insights.quote: The failure is not in building, but rather in scaling these PoCs to production scale and maintaining them.
insights.locator: The failure is not in building

insights.claim: 42% of healthcare AI buyers have completed or are running vendor consolidation, to simplify their stack (37%), reduce cost (32%) or remove vendors that fell short on security, compliance or performance (30%), while 57% feel inundated by point-solution pitches.
insights.speaker: Bessemer Venture Partners
insights.so_what: Point-solution vendors face churn; platforms consolidating budgets win.
insights.quote: Buyers have moved from evaluating capabilities to buying implementations, and most of the market is still selling the former.
insights.locator: Today, healthcare AI buyers want fewer

insights.claim: Share of healthcare AI development shifted toward healthcare-specific AI vendors (+12 p.p.) and AI labs (+2 p.p.) and away from internal building (-16 p.p.), with large HCIT incumbents also up 7 p.p., most visibly in provider RCM.
insights.speaker: Bessemer Venture Partners
insights.so_what: Healthcare-native AI startups are the biggest share winners; incumbents gain via embedded features in RCM.
insights.locator: Innovative healthcare AI vendors have taken

insights.claim: Winning healthcare AI companies like Abridge and SmarterDx scaled a wedge product into a platform, while Qventus won by providing co-development and deployment support, validating a land-and-expand playbook.
insights.speaker: Bessemer Venture Partners
insights.so_what: Back wedge-to-platform healthcare AI companies with co-development motions (note these are Bessemer portfolio names).
insights.quote: begin with a single product wedge, earn the workflow, then expand into adjacent products from inside
insights.locator: The companies that won scaled a wedge

insights.claim: Large HCIT and systems-of-record vendors capture low-hanging fruit by shipping off-the-shelf AI features into existing workflows without new procurement, making them real competitors today even though buyers look elsewhere for next-generation solutions.
insights.speaker: Bessemer Venture Partners
insights.so_what: Incumbents like EHR/RCM platforms are a near-term threat to startups but not the expected source of next-wave innovation.
insights.locator: Looking across individual use cases

insights.claim: Provider and payer AI rewards AI-native vendors that have solved regulated workflows, whereas pharma's highest-value problems are research problems where fine-tuned frontier model intelligence matters more, which is why AI labs gained most share in pharma.
insights.speaker: Bessemer Venture Partners
insights.so_what: AI labs are best positioned in life sciences; workflow-native startups in provider and payer.
insights.quote: Pharma's highest value problems are research problems, where the frontier model intelligence fine-tuned with proprietary data matters more than the wrapper around it.
insights.locator: Different segments need different types

themes.theme: AI-driven headcount reduction and labor shortage

insights.claim: Half of surveyed healthcare organizations have cut headcount due to AI or plan to within six months, averaging 8% to 13% of affected functions; applied to roughly $1 trillion of mostly labor admin spend, this implies about $100 billion in labor-spend dislocation.
insights.speaker: Bessemer Venture Partners
insights.so_what: A ~$100B labor-spend pool is the addressable savings for admin AI vendors.
insights.quote: taking a rough 10% of that suggests $100 billion in labor-spend dislocation
insights.locator: Where automation meets attrition trends

insights.claim: Among providers cutting staff, 73% name revenue cycle and medical billing; among payers, 71% name claims processing and 68% member services, while pharma is least likely to cut at 44%.
insights.speaker: Bessemer Venture Partners
insights.so_what: Workforce reductions track the highest-ROI functions, confirming where AI value is real.
insights.locator: The reductions follow the returns.

insights.claim: Healthcare has a shortage, not a surplus, of administrative workers: the American Medical Association puts the medical coder shortage at roughly 30%, the average certified coder is over 50, and certification plus ramp takes years.
insights.speaker: Bessemer Venture Partners
insights.so_what: AI is filling a structural labor gap, making admin automation demand durable rather than discretionary.
insights.quote: The American Medical Association puts the medical coder shortage at roughly 30%, and the average certified coder is over 50.
insights.locator: In reality, healthcare has no surplus

insights.claim: Because much administrative work is done by clinically trained staff such as prior-authorization and utilization-review nurses, automating those queues can redeploy them into care management roles organizations cannot currently hire into.
insights.speaker: Bessemer Venture Partners
insights.so_what: AI's value in healthcare includes capacity redeployment, not just FTE cuts.
insights.locator: Healthcare, like every other industry absorbing

insights.claim: About $1 trillion a year goes to US healthcare administration, with an estimated $260 billion considered waste, much of it the cost of payers and providers working against each other.
insights.speaker: Bessemer Venture Partners
insights.so_what: The largest admin prize sits in the payer-provider interface, not within single organizations.
insights.quote: This is the cost of two organizations working against each other.
insights.locator: The $1T opportunity

insights.claim: Denial and appeals management is providers' top pain point at 78% and prior authorization second at 61%, while appeals management is a top-three payer pain point at 42%, meaning the same dispute is staffed and paid for twice.
insights.speaker: Bessemer Venture Partners
insights.so_what: Tools addressing denials, appeals and prior auth address the most acute pain on both sides.
insights.quote: These are essentially the same dispute on both sides, staffed and paid for twice.
insights.locator: The pain point data makes this clear.

insights.claim: Current AI in prior authorization and utilization management amounts to AI-to-AI combat on mirrored workflows; the trillion-dollar value lies in eliminating the workflow via aligned incentives and real-time payments, requiring AI companies that serve both payers and providers.
insights.speaker: Bessemer Venture Partners
insights.so_what: Back interstitial platforms that serve both payers and providers rather than one-sided automation.
insights.quote: The near-term value is automation, and the trillion-dollar value is in making the workflow unnecessary.
insights.locator: This friction is also where AI

insights.claim: Care delivery costs around $3 trillion and grows about 5% per year, while the AAMC projects a shortfall of up to 86,000 physicians by 2036, including 20,200 to 40,400 in primary care.
insights.speaker: Bessemer Venture Partners
insights.so_what: Clinical AI addresses the largest and most supply-constrained spend pool in healthcare.
insights.locator: The $3T opportunity

insights.claim: Only 46% of respondents trust AI to support clinical decisions and 77% override its suggestions more than half the time; stronger clinical validation evidence (67%), transparent rationale (53%), patient-specific performance data (47%) and EHR integration (44%) would increase trust.
insights.speaker: Bessemer Venture Partners
insights.so_what: Vendors that build validation evidence and explainability can unlock clinical adoption.
insights.quote: Clinical AI is in the workflow without being relied on.
insights.locator: The first is trust.

insights.claim: 58% of providers say the treating clinician bears primary accountability for AI-influenced decisions and 50% cite medico-legal exposure as blocking scale past PoC, making the 77% override rate predictable rather than irrational.
insights.speaker: Bessemer Venture Partners
insights.so_what: Liability frameworks, not model accuracy, gate clinical AI scaling; watch for liability shifts.
insights.quote: It’s the predictable behavior of professionals who carry the risk personally.
insights.locator: Second, it’s liability.

insights.claim: 36% of providers have delayed or canceled clinical AI deployments over regulatory uncertainty, and there is no established regulatory path for pan-indication clinical intelligence or settled post-market monitoring regime for autonomous clinical AI.
insights.speaker: Bessemer Venture Partners
insights.so_what: Regulatory clarity is a key catalyst for clinical AI; until then deployments stall.
insights.locator: Third is regulatory and compliance.

insights.claim: Fee-for-service has no mechanism to pay for AI-delivered care; about 48% of payers are unwilling to reimburse fully autonomous AI care versus about 5% objecting to clinician-in-the-loop AI, making human-in-the-loop the reimbursable near-term architecture.
insights.speaker: Bessemer Venture Partners
insights.so_what: Near-term clinical AI business models should be clinician-in-the-loop to be reimbursable.
insights.quote: Human-in-the-loop is the reimbursable architecture for the near term.
insights.locator: Then, there’s payment.

insights.claim: Roughly 44% of payers are willing to establish payment pathways for AI in primary and preventive care, diagnostic support and medication management, and Bessemer expects CMS and national payers to move before the broader market follows.
insights.speaker: Bessemer Venture Partners
insights.so_what: CMS reimbursement decisions are a catalyst to watch for clinical AI vendors.
insights.quote: We expect CMS and the national payers will need to move before the broader market follows.
insights.locator: The good news is that payers

insights.claim: The US spends $500 billion a year on drugs and pharma spends $150 billion a year on R&D, but preclinical development, where most AI has focused, captures only 25% of R&D spend.
insights.speaker: Bessemer Venture Partners
insights.so_what: The bigger pharma AI prize is downstream in clinical trial success and access, not just discovery.
insights.quote: Preclinical development, which has been the focus of AI so far, captures only 25% of R&D spend.
insights.locator: The $0.5T drug development

insights.claim: As more AI-selected drug candidates enter the clinic, value shifts toward raising clinical trial success rates and widening patient access, which are earlier in ROI capture for structural rather than technical reasons.
insights.speaker: Bessemer Venture Partners
insights.so_what: Clinical-trial optimization and access tools are the next pharma AI frontier, with longer payback.
insights.locator: Preclinical development, which has been the focus

insights.claim: Agent harness infrastructure such as evals, performance monitoring, guardrails and orchestration maps almost exactly onto what clinicians need to trust AI and what regulators will require in post-market surveillance, so builders of this layer will scale past pilot more easily.
insights.speaker: Bessemer Venture Partners
insights.so_what: Healthcare AI vendors investing in evals and monitoring hold an edge in clinical scaling.
insights.quote: Those who build this layer deliberately will more easily scale past pilot in clinical and admin settings.
insights.locator: Outside of healthcare, teams deploying AI

insights.claim: Trust that sufficed for administrative AI is now the binding constraint on clinical deployment, so winners are companies building fast, expanding into adjacent workflows and compounding trust with enterprise partners.
insights.speaker: Bessemer Venture Partners
insights.so_what: Favor healthcare AI companies with deep enterprise relationships and proven trust records.
insights.quote: It’s wartime, and the biggest winners are the companies building fast, eating into adjacent workflows, and compounding trust with their enterprise partners.
insights.locator: What these opportunities tell builders and buyers
